name: Shoulder External Rotation (Rotator Cuff)
description: Outward rotation of the humerus about its long axis against resistance, training the posterior rotator cuff in its prime-mover role. Prime movers: infraspinatus and teres minor, with the supraspinatus assisting and (in the full-can/scaption variant) acting as an abductor at length. Exemplars: cable/band external rotation with the elbow pinned at the side, external rotation at 90-degree abduction (throwers' / 'L' position), side-lying dumbbell external rotation, full-can raise. A low-load prehab/accessory pattern that builds glenohumeral stability and balances the much stronger internal rotators.

name: Shoulder Internal Rotation (Rotator Cuff)
description: Inward rotation of the humerus about its long axis against resistance, training the anterior rotator cuff. Prime mover: subscapularis (the largest and strongest cuff muscle), with the pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, teres major, and anterior deltoid assisting as larger internal rotators. Exemplars: cable/band internal rotation with the elbow pinned at the side, lying dumbbell internal rotation. The direct antagonist of shoulder external rotation; typically far stronger, so trained for cuff balance and anterior-shoulder stability rather than size.

name: Scapular Protraction / Upward Rotation (Serratus Anterior)
description: Drawing the scapula forward around the ribcage (protraction) and rotating it upward, holding the shoulder blade flush to the thorax. Prime mover: serratus anterior (with the upper/lower trapezius co-acting as the force couple for upward rotation, and the pectoralis minor contributing to protraction/depression and scapular tilt). Exemplars: serratus punch / push-up-plus (scapular push-up), supine cable or dumbbell scapular protraction (closed- and open-chain reach-throughs), wall slide, overhead shrug. A scapular-control / prehab pattern; its antagonist is scapular retraction (the rear-delt / horizontal-pull family). Distinct from glenohumeral pressing because the elbows stay locked and the motion is pure scapular travel.

name: Hip Adduction
description: Drawing the femur back toward (and across) the midline in the frontal plane against resistance, training the hip adductor group (adductor longus/brevis/magnus, gracilis, pectineus). Exemplars: hip-adduction machine, standing cable hip adduction, Copenhagen plank/adduction, banded standing adduction. Sumo-stance squats, wide-stance leg press, and sumo deadlifts also load the adductors heavily as a knee-and-hip compound but are catalogued under squat/hinge; this pattern captures the dedicated frontal-plane adduction work. Contributes to frontal-plane pelvic and knee stability in single-leg and change-of-direction tasks.

name: Ankle Inversion / Eversion
description: Frontal-plane motion of the foot at the subtalar/ankle complex — inversion (sole turning inward, driven by tibialis posterior with tibialis anterior) and its antagonist eversion (sole turning outward, driven by the fibularis/peroneal group). These deep lower-leg muscles also act as dynamic medial/lateral ankle stabilizers and arch supporters during weight-bearing. Exemplars: banded ankle inversion, banded ankle eversion, and stabilizer-focused single-leg calf raises where the tibialis posterior and fibularis group control medial-lateral balance. Primarily a prehab/ankle-resilience pattern; inversion and eversion are mutual antagonists within the one pattern.
